episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is it better to be self-sufficient or well-connected?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [My Cariboo Now] Municipal elections nominations now open across the Cariboo and [My Cariboo Now] Errors in B.C. budget leave $1.5B hole in B.C.’s natural gas revenue forecast, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Should households and small businesses prioritize self-sufficient technical skills or rely on well-connected networks and institutional channels to stay secure against malware and security threats? Topics include: Geekom malware incident and repair culture response, Expired domain exploitation by threat actors and trust signals, Passkey security vulnerabilities and credential system limitations, Infrastructure gaps between urban and rural security information access, Local computer repair shops as informal security intelligence nodes, Educational programs like SD27 trades training as long-term capacity building.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: School District 27 (Cariboo-Chilcotin)

discussion.central_question: Should households and small businesses prioritize self-sufficient technical skills or rely on well-connected networks and institutional channels to stay secure against malware and security threats?
discussion.riley_position: Neither self-sufficiency nor institutional trust works alone; security requires both individual competence and community-level intelligence networks feeding information back and forth across multiple nodes.
riley_key_evidence: Geekom's malware fix was caught quickly because engaged users in the company's support ecosystem flagged the compromised driver file before it spread
Threat actor schemes like Sable Squirrel buying 10,000 expired domains (costing $7M) are only discovered through researchers pooling intelligence across thousands of sightings at once
Passkey vulnerabilities still require clean devices first—the maintenance burden never disappears, it just gets reframed
discussion.casey_position: Rural communities lack access to network-level threat intelligence that urban areas receive through institutional channels; the actual gap is not funding but a structural wiring problem of who serves as the local information node.
casey_key_evidence: A small business in Wells running budget hardware doesn't have in-house IT to check signatures daily, making them dependent on whoever runs the local repair shop
Geekom's official support page was itself the compromised source—the trusted channel became the vector
Passkeys were marketed as a fix-it-once solution that removes user vigilance, but no credential system actually achieves that
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed that individual skills and network-level intelligence are complementary layers rather than competing options, and identified a concrete local solution: a regional one-page monthly bulletin distributed through existing business associations to surface current threats and fixes without formal funding.
